stem: Consultant Priya Raman describes her practice as person-centered. At their first meeting, collegiate swimmer Tomasz Wójcik asks, "So how does this work? Do you give me a program to follow?" Which explanation of the process is most consistent with Priya's theoretical orientation?
options: "You'll pick the goals, and I'll teach you mental skills matched to them to practice."
"We'll explore the thoughts behind your nerves and test new ones between sessions."
"You'll lead the conversation; my part is to understand your experience as you see it."
"You'll describe what you want instead, and we'll build on times it already happens."
rationales: Letting the client choose goals is collaborative, but the consultant still supplies a skills curriculum. That is a mental skills training model with the consultant as technical expert, not the nondirective, relationship-driven process of person-centered work.
Examining the thoughts behind nerves and testing alternatives between sessions describes a cognitive-behavioral process, which is structured and consultant-guided rather than person-centered.

Person-centered practice (Rogers) treats the client as the expert on his own experience and relies on the relationship itself, built on empathy, unconditional positive regard, and genuineness, to support self-directed growth. Explaining the process this way sets accurate expectations for that kind of work.

Defining a preferred future and building on times it already happens describes a solution-focused process. It is client-centered in tone, but it steers the conversation toward exceptions and solutions rather than following the client's own exploration.
takeaway: A person-centered consultant explains the work as client-directed and relationship-driven, not as a prescribed program.

stem: Lena Okafor's consulting practice is grounded in feminist approaches. She begins working with Marisol Vega, an elite rugby player who says earlier consultants "talked at me and decided what I needed." Which first-session action is most consistent with Lena's approach to building the working relationship?
options: Explain how she works and why, and invite Marisol to challenge it and help shape the focus
Give a standardized mental skills inventory, then share the profile to set the session focus
Keep her own values out of the sessions so that Marisol's choices are not influenced by them
Meet with Marisol and her coach together so that all three can agree on the session focus
rationales: Feminist approaches build an egalitarian relationship: the consultant demystifies the process by explaining methods and their rationale, treats the client as an expert on her own life, and shares decisions about the work. That directly answers Marisol's experience of being talked at.

Sharing assessment results is good practice, but letting an inventory set the focus keeps the consultant and the instrument in the expert role. It does not address the power imbalance Marisol describes or invite her to shape the work.

Feminist approaches reject the idea that consulting is value-neutral; they favor being open about one's values so the client can weigh them. Aiming for strict neutrality also does nothing to share power in the relationship.

Coach input can matter, but bringing a third party into the first decision about focus repeats the pattern of others deciding for her. A feminist consultant would first establish an egalitarian relationship with Marisol herself.
takeaway: Feminist practice builds an egalitarian relationship: demystify the process and share decisions with the client.

stem: A youth soccer academy hires consultant Daniel Whitfield to help a 12-year-old player whose performance has dropped since her parents separated. Daniel works from an ecological systems perspective. When he explains his process to the academy director, which description best reflects that perspective?
options: "I'll build her focus, confidence, and coping skills one-on-one so she can handle home stress."
"I'll help her identify the beliefs behind her decline and, with consent, update her coach."
"I'll refer the family to a counselor for the separation and keep my sessions on her soccer."
"I'll look at how home, school, and the club affect her and, with consent, involve key adults."
rationales: Individual skill building can help, but it treats the problem as located solely in the player. An ecological consultant would not plan to work around her home life; the family transition is part of what needs to be understood.

Updating the coach with consent is appropriate, but the core of this plan is identifying and changing her beliefs, which is a cognitive-behavioral, individual-level explanation of the decline rather than an ecological one.

A counseling referral may be useful for the family, but splitting home off from her soccer work treats her settings as separate compartments. The ecological view is that her performance emerges from how those settings interact.

An ecological systems perspective (Bronfenbrenner) holds that development and performance are shaped by interacting settings such as family, school, and club. Explaining that these settings and the key adults in them are part of the work, with consent, reflects that view and sets expectations for the director.
takeaway: From a systems view, the consultant explains up front that the client's settings and key adults are part of the work.

stem: At intake, professional golfer Hiroshi Tanaka says, "I need you to get rid of my nerves on the first tee." His consultant, Anika Brandt, works from the Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) approach. Which explanation of the work ahead is most consistent with that approach?
options: "We'll build a breathing routine that brings your arousal down before each opening shot."
"We'll practice noticing the nerves without fighting them as you commit to each shot."
"We'll examine what the nerves are telling you and practice more helpful ways to read them."
"We'll find the intensity level where you play best and build a routine to help you reach it."
rationales: Lowering arousal with breathing is a sound regulation technique, but it pursues the same goal Hiroshi brought in: changing or reducing the internal state. MAC instead shifts the aim away from controlling the nerves.

The Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment approach (Gardner and Moore) holds that performance improves when athletes accept internal states such as nerves without trying to control them and keep attention on task-relevant, values-consistent action.

Reappraising what the nerves mean is a cognitive-behavioral strategy: it works to change the content of the interpretation, whereas MAC changes the athlete's relationship to the experience without disputing it.
Finding an individual optimal intensity reflects IZOF-style arousal regulation. It is evidence-based, but it still aims to manage the internal state into a target zone rather than accept it.
takeaway: MAC reframes the goal from eliminating uncomfortable states to accepting them while committing to performance-relevant action.

stem: Executive Olivia Grant asks consultant Marcus Bell how their sessions will run. He replies, "Each time, we'll set an agenda together, look at how your interpretations of high-stakes meetings shape how you feel and act, and agree on something to try before the next session." Which theoretical orientation does Marcus's explanation best reflect?
options: Person-centered
Cognitive-behavioral
Acceptance and commitment
Solution-focused
rationales: A person-centered consultant would not set structured agendas or assign between-session tasks; the process is nondirective and driven by the relationship.

Collaborative agenda setting, a focus on how interpretations of situations shape emotions and behavior (the cognitive model), and between-session practice are hallmarks of cognitive-behavioral work (Beck).
ACT also uses between-session practice, but it targets the client's relationship to thoughts and values-based action rather than examining how particular interpretations drive feelings and behavior.
Solution-focused work centers on exceptions, preferred futures, and scaling rather than on analyzing how interpretations produce emotional reactions.
takeaway: Structured agendas, the thought–feeling–behavior link, and between-session practice signal a cognitive-behavioral orientation.

stem: Police sergeant Ray Delgado tells consultant Aisha Mensah, "During the standoff I froze for a few seconds. My partner covered for me. Now I keep wondering whether I can be trusted out there." Aisha works from a person-centered orientation. Which response best communicates accurate empathy?
options: "Brief freezing under extreme threat is a common stress response, even among veteran officers."
"It sounds like you want to feel ready; let's build a breathing routine for calls that escalate."
"Help me understand what was happening for you in the seconds just before you froze."
"Since those few seconds, you've been doubting whether you can rely on yourself out there."
rationales: Normalizing may be accurate and well meant, but reassurance moves away from his felt experience and can signal that his concern should be set aside rather than understood.

It opens with a brief reflection but quickly turns to a technique. In a person-centered frame, conveying understanding of his experience comes before any problem solving, and the advice shifts the focus to the consultant's agenda.
An open invitation to explore is respectful, but it asks for details of the event rather than communicating that the consultant already grasps what the event means to him.

Accurate empathy (Rogers) means sensing the client's inner world and communicating that understanding back. This reflection captures the meaning he has drawn (doubting he can rely on himself) and the ongoing weight of it, which builds the working relationship.
takeaway: Accurate empathy reflects the client's felt meaning back to them; reassurance, advice, and fact-finding do not.

stem: Consultant Jordan Avery's written philosophy states that the aim of consulting is athlete self-reliance: athletes should learn to use mental skills without depending on the consultant. At a first meeting, a collegiate volleyball coach asks how Jordan will work with the team this season. Which description of Jordan's role is most consistent with that philosophy?
options: "I'll teach the skills early, then gradually hand responsibility for using them to the players."
"I'll attend matches and help players settle during timeouts, then debrief with them afterward."
"I'll offer drop-in sessions so players can come to me whenever a problem starts to build."
"I'll design an individual routine for each player and review how they're using it each week."
rationales: A philosophy of practice (Poczwardowski and colleagues) links core beliefs to the consultant's role and methods. A self-reliance aim implies an educational role: teach the skills, then fade the consultant's involvement so athletes own their use.

Match support and debriefs can be valuable, but if the consultant is the one settling players during timeouts, they learn to rely on the consultant in the moments that matter most, which runs against the stated aim.
Accessible drop-in support is well meant, but a reactive, consultant-centered service invites players to bring problems to the consultant rather than building their own capacity to handle them.
Individual routines can be effective, but having the consultant design and monitor them keeps ownership with the consultant. The philosophy calls for transferring that responsibility to the players.
takeaway: The role a consultant describes should follow from their core beliefs; a self-reliance philosophy implies teaching and then handing over responsibility.

stem: In a video call, professional esports player Malik Haddad asks how working with consultant Sofia Lindqvist will help with the tilt he experiences after losing early rounds. Sofia uses a solution-focused approach. Which explanation of her process is most consistent with that approach?
options: "We'll trace the tilt back to its roots so you understand why it started in the first place."
"We'll identify the beliefs behind the tilt, then test them against what happens in games."
"We'll get clear on what you want instead, find times you already recover, and build on those."
"We'll learn to notice the frustration without struggling against it as you keep playing."
rationales: Tracing the origins of a problem reflects insight-oriented approaches. Solution-focused practice deliberately spends little time analyzing a problem's causes.

Identifying beliefs and testing them against real outcomes is a cognitive-behavioral process. It focuses on the problem's maintaining thoughts rather than on the client's preferred future and existing successes.

Solution-focused practice (de Shazer) is future- and strengths-oriented: it clarifies the client's preferred outcome, looks for exceptions (times the problem is absent or smaller), and builds on what already works.
Noticing frustration without struggling against it while staying engaged in play describes an acceptance-based process such as ACT or MAC.
takeaway: Solution-focused consultants explain the work as building on exceptions and the client's preferred future, not analyzing the problem.

stem: A high school basketball coach refers 16-year-old Devon Harris to consultant Rachel Kim because he "won't do the team's pre-game routine." With his parent's permission and Devon's assent in place, Rachel meets him. Devon says the routine is pointless and he sees no reason to change anything. Using the transtheoretical model, which approach to this first session fits best?
options: Set a small, specific goal for him to try one part of the routine before this week's game
Review the pros and cons of the routine with him, then ask him to commit to a trial week
Build rapport, then ask him to pick one part of the routine he could try this week
Build rapport and explore his views on game preparation, leaving change plans for later
rationales: A small, specific goal is a good action-stage tool, but Devon sees no reason to change. Setting behavioral goals before he is even considering change mismatches his stage and is likely to increase resistance.
Weighing pros and cons suits someone who is already ambivalent, and asking for a commitment fits preparation. For a precontemplator, both steps move faster than he is ready to go.

Building rapport is the right start, but moving straight to choosing a part of the routine to try asks for action from someone who does not yet see a reason to change. In precontemplation, the work is understanding his view and raising awareness, not selecting a first step.

The transtheoretical model matches strategy to stage. Devon sees no reason to change, which marks precontemplation, so the first session should build rapport and gently raise awareness by understanding his perspective, leaving action planning until he is considering change.
takeaway: With a precontemplator, match the stage: build rapport and raise awareness before asking for action.

stem: Two consultants with similar years of experience work with the same university's teams, and both use goal setting and imagery. One presents herself as an expert who diagnoses weaknesses and prescribes fixes; the other presents herself as a collaborator who helps athletes find their own solutions. According to frameworks for a professional philosophy of practice, what best explains this difference in how they relate to clients?
options: They differ in session structure, such as the length, frequency, and format they use
They differ in their underlying beliefs about people, change, and the consultant's role
They differ in how much experience they have, since an expert style develops with practice
They differ in the demands of the sports and competitive levels their athletes compete at
rationales: Session length, frequency, and format are delivery choices that follow from a philosophy. They describe how the work is packaged, not why one consultant takes an expert stance and the other a collaborative one.

Frameworks for a philosophy of practice (Poczwardowski and colleagues) place core beliefs and values about people, behavior change, and the consultant's role at the foundation. Those beliefs shape how a consultant relates to clients even when the techniques are identical.
The stem says the two have similar years of experience, so experience cannot explain the difference. Expert and collaborative stances are found at every career stage.
Both consultants serve the same university's teams, so sport and level are held constant. The difference lies in what each believes about clients and the consultant's role.
takeaway: Same techniques and setting, different roles: the difference lives in core beliefs, the foundation of a philosophy of practice.

stem: Consultant Ben Asante works from a structured cognitive-behavioral model with set goals, agendas, and between-session practice. At an initial meeting, masters marathoner Ingrid Solberg, 58, says she wants open-ended conversations to make sense of what running means to her as she nears the end of her competitive career. What should Ben do first?
options: Describe how he works and discuss openly whether that fits what Ingrid is seeking
Explain his model briefly, then start his program and review the fit with her after two sessions
Adapt to an open-ended, nondirective style for her, since the client's preference should lead
Refer her to a colleague who offers open-ended work, since her goals differ from his model
rationales: A clearly articulated philosophy lets a consultant describe their approach transparently at intake. Discussing fit openly respects Ingrid's informed choice and is the necessary first step before deciding whether to proceed, adapt, or refer.

Explaining the model is a good start, but beginning the program anyway, when she has already said she wants something different, puts the method ahead of her stated goals and her informed choice. Fit should be discussed before the work begins, not reviewed afterward.
Responding to client preference is important, but abruptly adopting a nondirective style he is not trained in risks practicing outside his competence and abandons a coherent philosophy of practice.
A referral may turn out to be right, but making it before he has explained his approach and talked with her about fit is premature; she may value elements of his work or clarify what she wants.
takeaway: A clear philosophy lets a consultant describe their approach transparently so the client can judge fit before the work begins.

stem: Reviewing recordings of virtual sessions with wheelchair tennis player Camila Reyes, a supervisor notices that consultant Theo Nguyen, who identifies as person-centered, becomes warm and animated when Camila reports wins but noticeably cooler and more distant when she describes losses or setbacks. Which of Rogers's conditions is Theo most clearly failing to provide?
options: Accurate empathic understanding
Congruence, or genuineness
Unconditional positive regard
Psychological contact
rationales: Empathy concerns understanding the client's inner experience. The pattern described is not mainly a failure to understand Camila; it is acceptance that shifts with how she performs.
Congruence means the consultant's outward expression matches his inner experience. Nothing suggests Theo is masking his feelings; the problem is that his regard depends on her results.

Unconditional positive regard (Rogers) is acceptance of the client that does not depend on what she reports or achieves. Warmth that rises with wins and fades with losses communicates conditional worth and can teach Camila to hide setbacks.
Psychological contact, meaning that the two are in a relationship in which each affects the other, is clearly present. The issue is the conditional quality of Theo's regard.
takeaway: Warmth that tracks results is conditional regard; unconditional positive regard accepts the person regardless of performance.

stem: Consultant Grace Liu takes an ecological systems approach. With his guardian's permission and his assent in place, she begins assessing Mateo Ruiz, a 14-year-old figure skater whose jumps have become inconsistent this season. Which assessment question best reflects Grace's theoretical approach?
options: "What goes through your mind as you set up for a jump you've been missing?"
"How have things changed this year among the people in your life on and off the ice?"
"On a scale of 1 to 10, where are your jumps now, and what would one step higher look like?"
"How confident are you, right now, that you can land each jump in your program?"
rationales: Asking about thoughts during setup targets cognitive appraisals, the starting point of a cognitive-behavioral assessment rather than an ecological one.

An ecological systems approach (Bronfenbrenner) assesses the athlete within interacting settings and relationships, such as family, school, and the rink, so it asks how things have shifted among the people across those settings.
A scaling question with a next-step follow-up is a solution-focused technique; it tracks progress rather than mapping the athlete's environments.
Rating confidence for specific jumps assesses task-specific self-efficacy, an individual-level variable, without exploring the systems around the athlete.
takeaway: Ecological assessment maps how the athlete's settings (family, school, sport) interact, not just individual thoughts or ratings.

stem: Orchestral trumpet player Nadia Petrova tells consultant Samuel Osei that her hands shake and her chest tightens before auditions. Samuel works from a cognitive-behavioral model and wants to understand what keeps these reactions going. Which assessment question best fits his model?
options: "When you notice your hands shaking backstage, what do you tell yourself it means?"
"Tell me about an audition when the shaking was milder. What was different that day?"
"How do your family and teachers talk about auditions, and how does that affect you?"
"Which values do you want to bring into the audition room, whatever you're feeling?"
rationales: The cognitive model (Beck) holds that emotional and physical reactions are shaped by how a person interprets situations and sensations. Asking what she tells herself the shaking means identifies the automatic thoughts and appraisals that may be maintaining her anxiety.
Searching for exceptions, times when the problem was smaller, is a solution-focused assessment strategy that builds on what works rather than mapping the thoughts that maintain the problem.
Asking how family and teachers talk about auditions explores her social system. It can add context, but it is a systems question rather than a cognitive-behavioral one.
Clarifying values to carry into performance regardless of feelings is an acceptance and commitment strategy, which works on her relationship to inner experience rather than on her appraisals.
takeaway: CBT assessment asks what the client believes a situation or sensation means, linking appraisals to emotions and behavior.

stem: A college athletic department asks consultant Elena Vasquez why many athletes skip the injury-prevention warm-up designed by the sports medicine staff. Elena will build her questionnaire and focus-group questions around the theory of planned behavior. Which set of topics should those questions cover?
options: Which stage of change each athlete is in, from precontemplation to maintenance
How competent, autonomous, and connected to teammates athletes feel in warm-ups
How susceptible athletes feel to injury and how severe they think an injury would be
Athletes' attitudes toward it, what others expect, and how much control they feel they have
rationales: Stages of change come from the transtheoretical model. They describe readiness but are not the determinants of intention specified by the theory of planned behavior.
Competence, autonomy, and relatedness are the basic psychological needs of self-determination theory, a different motivational framework.
Perceived susceptibility and severity are constructs from the health belief model, not the theory of planned behavior.

The theory of planned behavior (Ajzen) holds that attitudes toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control shape intention, which in turn predicts behavior. Assessment should therefore target these determinants, along with intention itself.
takeaway: TPB assessment targets attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control as the drivers of intention.

stem: Assessment with collegiate pole vaulter Amara Diallo shows that she treats thoughts like "I'll balk again" as facts, works hard to push them out of her mind, and has begun skipping high-pressure meets. She says she vaults because she loves the challenge. Her consultant, Felix Romero, works from acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT). Which plan best fits an ACT interpretation of these data?
options: Clarify her values first, then return her to meets once the balking thoughts are less frequent
Weigh the evidence for and against each balking thought, then test it at a practice meet
Build her willingness to have the thoughts and defuse from them as she returns to meets
Teach a pre-vault centering routine so that she can clear the thoughts before each attempt
rationales: Values work belongs in an ACT plan, but making her return to meets contingent on the thoughts decreasing keeps the control agenda that ACT targets. In ACT, values-based action proceeds with the thoughts present.
Weighing evidence and testing a thought is cognitive restructuring. It treats the thought's content as the problem, whereas ACT addresses fusion with the thought rather than its accuracy.

ACT (Hayes) interprets treating thoughts as facts as cognitive fusion and pushing thoughts away and skipping meets as experiential avoidance. Building willingness and defusion while returning to valued action targets both processes and links to her stated value of loving the challenge.

A centering routine is a useful pre-performance tool, but using it to clear the thoughts is another attempt to control internal experience, which an ACT conceptualization identifies as part of the problem.
takeaway: ACT reads 'thoughts as facts' and avoidance as fusion and experiential avoidance, and plans acceptance, defusion, and values-based action.

stem: Intake data show that firefighter Owen Gallagher sleeps poorly between shifts. He says, "I know I should change my pre-sleep habits, maybe in the next few months, but I'm not sure it's worth giving up my late-night gaming." Using the transtheoretical model to plan, which focus best fits his current stage?
options: A detailed sleep schedule with a nightly log, starting tonight, to build the new habits
Identifying with him the high-risk nights, such as after hard calls, and how to protect sleep
Setting a firm start date within the next two weeks and telling his crew about the plan
Exploring with him what he would gain and lose by changing, and what would tip the balance
rationales: A detailed schedule and log are action-stage tools. Owen is still ambivalent and is thinking about change only in the coming months, so an immediate program skips the work his stage calls for.
Anticipating high-risk situations is relapse-prevention work suited to people who have already changed and are maintaining it. Owen has not yet started.

Setting a firm date and making a public commitment are preparation-stage strategies for someone intending to act within about a month. Owen's 'maybe in the next few months' and his doubt that it is worth it place him earlier.

In the transtheoretical model, Owen's intention to change within months, combined with ambivalence, marks contemplation. Decisional balance work, exploring the pros and cons of change and what would shift it, helps resolve that ambivalence and move him toward preparation.
takeaway: For a client in contemplation, plan around decisional balance and resolving ambivalence, not an immediate action program.

stem: Leah Brooks, the only woman on her firm's trading desk, tells consultant Hana Ito that she has stopped sharing ideas in strategy meetings because they are "usually brushed off," and she blames herself for "not being assertive enough." Hana works from a feminist approach. Which interpretation of this information best fits that approach?
options: Her silence reflects the desk's norms about whose ideas count, not simply a personal deficit
Her self-blame reflects an all-or-nothing thinking pattern to examine with her in sessions
Her silence reflects an assertiveness skills gap that targeted training could help her close
Her self-blame reflects low confidence built up through setbacks earlier in her career
rationales: Feminist approaches hold that the personal is political: individual distress is understood in its sociocultural context, including gender and power. Reading her silence as a response to the desk's norms counters self-blame without denying her agency.

Examining thinking patterns collaboratively is a cognitive-behavioral conceptualization. It locates the problem in her cognition and can reinforce self-blame by overlooking how the environment responds to her.
Assertiveness skills may help her later, but framing the issue as her deficit puts the problem entirely inside her. A feminist conceptualization first asks how the context is shaping her behavior.

Career history may play some part, but this interpretation stays at the individual level and ignores the current, observable pattern of her ideas being brushed off on a desk where she is the only woman.
takeaway: Feminist conceptualization places individual struggles in sociocultural context, examining power and gender rather than defaulting to self-blame.

stem: Consultant Raj Patel is helping a tech company plan an employee exercise initiative. His theory of planned behavior survey shows that employees rate exercise as highly worthwhile and believe managers and coworkers approve of it, yet most report weak intentions and say back-to-back meetings leave no realistic window for a workout. Which planning priority best follows from these results?
options: A campaign highlighting the health and work-performance benefits of regular exercise
Protected time on calendars and short workouts that fit between scheduled meetings
Senior-leader endorsements signaling that the company values employee exercise
Goal-setting workshops in which employees commit to a specific weekly exercise target
rationales: Attitudes are already favorable, so a benefits campaign targets a determinant that is not the problem.

In the theory of planned behavior (Ajzen), intention depends on attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. Attitudes and norms are already strong here; the weak link is control, so structural supports such as protected time and short sessions should come first.
Employees already believe managers and coworkers approve, so more endorsements target subjective norms, which are already high.
Goal setting can strengthen follow-through once people intend to act, but asking for a weekly commitment does not remove the scheduling barrier that is keeping intentions weak in the first place.
takeaway: Use TPB data diagnostically: target whichever determinant (attitude, norm, or perceived control) is weak.

stem: A collegiate hockey coach asks consultant Mira Hoffman to "fix" the starting goalie's anxiety. Her observations show a repeating pattern: after an early goal against, the coach yells at the defense, defenders play tentatively, more shots reach the goalie, his anxiety rises, and the coach yells louder. Mira works from a systems perspective. Which interpretation should guide her plan?
options: The goalie's anxiety drives the cycle, so building his coping skills should come first
The coach's reactions start the cycle, so changing his bench communication should come first
Each link sustains the others, so the plan should target the cycle as a whole
Weak team cohesion drives the cycle, so team-building for the whole roster should come first
rationales: Coping skills may help the goalie, but treating his anxiety as the driver accepts the coach's linear framing. In a systems view his anxiety is one link in the loop, and changing it alone leaves the rest of the pattern intact.

The coach's behavior is an important link, but naming it as the starting point is still linear cause-and-effect thinking. A systems view sees the yelling as both a cause and a result of what happens on the ice.

A systems perspective uses circular rather than linear causality: each person's behavior is both a response to and a trigger for the others. Planning around the whole cycle, involving coach, defense, and goalie, is how a systems-oriented consultant interrupts it.

Team-building works at the group level, but the observations show a specific interaction sequence among coach, defense, and goalie, not low cohesion. A general social intervention would not interrupt the cycle that keeps the goalie's anxiety going.
takeaway: Systems thinking replaces 'who is the cause?' with 'what cycle keeps this going?' and intervenes on the cycle.

stem: Consultant Zoe Adler's written philosophy states that performance problems are maintained by how athletes interpret events and that her role is to help athletes become skilled at questioning those interpretations themselves. After assessing professional soccer player Luis Ortega, who reports harsh self-criticism after mistakes, she is drafting his plan. Which plan is most consistent with her philosophy of practice?
options: Teach Luis to log his post-mistake thoughts and weigh the evidence for and against them
Teach Luis to notice his self-critical thoughts and let them pass without engaging them
Give Luis a set of confident statements to repeat after mistakes in place of the criticism
Review his mistakes with him on video, then build a reset routine he can use on the pitch
rationales: Her philosophy names interpretations as the maintaining factor and the consultant's role as teaching athletes to examine them. Teaching Luis to record and evaluate his own thoughts (cognitive restructuring, Beck) applies both beliefs directly, so the plan follows from the philosophy.

Noticing and letting thoughts pass is an acceptance-based strategy. It can reduce the grip of self-criticism, but it deliberately avoids evaluating the thoughts, which is the skill her philosophy says she is there to teach.

Replacement statements target his thinking, but the consultant supplies the new content instead of teaching Luis to question his interpretations, so the plan does not build the self-evaluation skill her philosophy emphasizes.
Video review and a reset routine are useful behavioral tools, but they work on what he does after mistakes rather than on the interpretations her philosophy identifies as the source of the problem.
takeaway: A consistent plan follows from the consultant's beliefs about what maintains problems and what the consultant's role is.

stem: Collegiate diver Bianca Moretti believes, "If I don't feel completely calm on the board, I'll miss the dive." She now repeats her breathing routine until she feels calm, often delaying long after her coach signals her to go. Her consultant, Isaac Levin, uses cognitive-behavioral methods and wants to test this belief in practice. Which next step is most consistent with that approach?
options: Help her shorten the breathing routine so that she reaches calm sooner before each dive
Review evidence with her that many divers score well without feeling calm on the board
Teach her a cue word to refocus on the takeoff whenever she notices nerves on the board
Have her predict, then perform, practice dives while still nervous, and compare results
rationales: Making the routine more efficient still treats feeling calm as a requirement. It keeps the safety behavior in place, so the belief that she must feel calm to dive well never gets tested.
Discussing evidence is a cognitive-behavioral move, but it is verbal rather than experiential. The consultant wants to test the belief in practice, which calls for a behavioral experiment.
A refocusing cue can help attention, but it does not test her prediction about what happens when she dives without feeling calm, so the belief itself goes unexamined.

A behavioral experiment (Beck) tests a belief directly: the client states a prediction, acts without the safety behavior (here, diving while still nervous), and compares the outcome with the prediction. Disconfirming evidence from her own experience is more persuasive than reassurance.
takeaway: Behavioral experiments test a belief by having the client predict, act without safety behaviors, and compare the results.

stem: During a session, wheelchair basketball player Kofi Boateng rates his confidence at the free-throw line as 4 out of 10. His consultant, Elif Demir, uses a solution-focused approach. Which follow-up to the rating is most consistent with how that approach uses scaling questions?
options: "What would a 10 look like, and how will you get there this week?"
"What would you notice yourself doing differently at a 5?"
"When did your confidence at the line first start to slip?"
"What thoughts tend to go through your mind at a 4?"
rationales: Describing a 10 borrows solution-focused language about the preferred future, but asking how to reach it this week jumps to the top of the scale in one leap. Solution-focused scaling uses the rating to define the next small, achievable step, so the move to a 5 is the better follow-up here.

Solution-focused scaling (de Shazer) uses the client's own rating to define one small next step in concrete, observable terms. Asking what he would notice himself doing at a 5 keeps the conversation on progress and makes change feel achievable.
Exploring when the problem began is problem-history work; solution-focused consultants spend little time on a problem's origins.
Assessing the thoughts that accompany low confidence is a cognitive-behavioral move. It focuses on what maintains the problem rather than on signs of progress.
takeaway: In solution-focused work, a scaling rating is a springboard to the next small, observable step.

topic: Feminist empowerment in a team session
stem: During a team session, players on a collegiate women's ice hockey team say they receive far less ice time and worse practice slots than the men's team. They feel powerless about it, though several say they would push for change if they knew how. Their consultant, Naomi Barrett, works from a feminist approach. Which response during the session is most consistent with that approach?
options: Acknowledge their frustration, then guide them back to the controllables for upcoming games
Raise the inequity with the athletic director herself, then report back to the team on it
Validate the inequity as real and help them plan how to raise it through proper channels
Explore how each player's beliefs about the situation are adding to their sense of powerlessness
rationales: Focusing on controllables is a common performance strategy, but steering away from a real inequity treats it as a distraction and leaves the players' sense of powerlessness untouched.

Advocacy has a place in feminist practice, but taking the issue up on the players' behalf, when they have said they want to act themselves, rescues them rather than empowering them and keeps the power with the consultant.

Feminist approaches validate that clients' distress can reflect real structural inequities and emphasize empowerment: helping clients recognize their power and act on their own behalf. Supporting the players to raise the issue themselves does both.
Examining beliefs is a cognitive-behavioral move. Here it risks locating the problem in the players' thinking when the inequity they describe is an external, structural one.
takeaway: Feminist practice validates real inequities and empowers clients to act for themselves, rather than reframing the issue away or rescuing them.

stem: After one poor training flight, military flight student Rohan Mehta tells consultant Dana Whitaker, "I'm definitely going to wash out of this program." Dana is using cognitive restructuring and wants Rohan to learn to reappraise thoughts like this on his own. Which next step is most consistent with that technique?
options: Ask him what in his training record supports and contradicts that prediction
Point out the catastrophizing and offer him a more balanced statement to rehearse
Invite him to notice the thought without judgment and refocus on his values
Have him use a confident self-talk cue each time the prediction comes to mind
rationales: Cognitive restructuring in CBT (Beck) uses guided discovery: Socratic questions about the evidence for and against an automatic thought help the client reach a more balanced appraisal himself, which builds the skill Dana wants him to use on his own.

Naming the distortion and offering a balanced alternative is a recognizable restructuring step, but the consultant supplies the answer. Rohan learns her reappraisal rather than how to reach one himself.
Noticing a thought nonjudgmentally and returning to values is an acceptance-based (ACT) strategy, which changes his relationship to the thought rather than evaluating its accuracy.
A self-talk cue can help in the moment, but it swaps one unexamined statement for another. Restructuring aims for balanced, evidence-based thinking that he arrives at by examining the thought.
takeaway: Cognitive restructuring examines the evidence for a thought through guided discovery, not by decree or affirmation.

stem: Midway through races, masters triathlete Gwen Holloway, 61, gets caught up in the thought "I'm too old for this," and her pace drops. Her consultant, Pavel Novak, uses acceptance and commitment therapy and wants to teach her cognitive defusion. Which technique best fits that aim?
options: Listing evidence that she is still fit and competitive in her age group
Saying "Stop" silently and switching to a confident cue word instead
Turning her attention to her stroke and breathing as soon as the thought shows up
Restating it as "I'm having the thought that I'm too old" and carrying on
rationales: Gathering counterevidence is cognitive restructuring. It disputes the thought's content, whereas defusion leaves the content alone and changes her relationship to it.
Thought stopping followed by a replacement cue tries to suppress the thought, which ACT views as experiential control that can make thoughts more persistent.
Shifting attention to the task can help, but using it to get away from the thought is distraction rather than defusion. Defusion means seeing the thought as a thought while it is present.

Cognitive defusion in ACT (Hayes) helps a person see a thought as a passing mental event rather than a literal truth. Prefacing it with 'I'm having the thought that…' creates that distance without disputing or suppressing it, so she can keep racing.
takeaway: Defusion changes the client's relationship to a thought by seeing it as a thought, without disputing or suppressing it.

stem: Andre Lefebvre exercised four times a week for eight months until a family move disrupted his routine three weeks ago. He tells consultant Lucia Ferraro that he feels like a failure but wants to restart next week. Applying the transtheoretical model, what is the most appropriate response in this session?
options: Revisit his reasons for exercising with a decisional balance exercise before planning a restart
Set a weekly target that matches his old routine so that he picks up where he left off
Normalize the lapse as common in change and plan his restart around strategies that worked
Explore his sense of failure first, and leave restart planning for a later session
rationales: Decisional balance suits clients who are still ambivalent. Andre already wants to restart next week, so going back to weighing reasons misreads his readiness and slows him down.
Returning straight to his old volume ignores the disruption and his sense of failure; an ambitious target after a lapse raises the risk of another setback. Restarts usually build back gradually.

The transtheoretical model treats lapse and relapse as a normal part of change, often with recycling through stages. Normalizing the lapse reduces self-blame, and planning around strategies that worked before matches his readiness to act.

Attending to his feelings matters, but postponing planning when he is ready to restart next week misses the opportunity. Normalizing the lapse can address the failure feeling and planning can happen in the same session.
takeaway: TTM treats relapse as part of change: normalize it, match the client's current readiness, and re-engage proven strategies.

stem: Partway through a planned imagery session, collegiate rower Imani Carter becomes tearful and says she can't concentrate because her father was just diagnosed with a serious illness. She shows no signs of risk to herself. Her consultant, Erik Sandberg, works from a person-centered orientation. What is the most consistent next move?
options: Acknowledge her news briefly, then offer a shorter imagery script so the session still helps
Set the imagery aside and reflect what she is feeling, letting her lead the conversation
Acknowledge her distress and give her information about counseling services for grief
Help her plan how to balance visits to her father with her training and classes
rationales: Shortening the script is a considerate adjustment, but it still puts the planned agenda ahead of what she has brought. A person-centered consultant follows the client's immediate experience.

Person-centered practice (Rogers) follows the client's lead and offers empathy, acceptance, and genuineness. When she brings something this significant, setting the plan aside and reflecting her feelings is the most consistent response.
Sharing counseling information may be useful later, but she shows no risk and is having a normal reaction to hard news. Moving to resources now redirects her before she has been heard.
Practical planning may help eventually, but it shifts to problem solving that the consultant leads, rather than staying with her emotional experience as a person-centered orientation calls for.
takeaway: When a client brings something important, a person-centered consultant sets the agenda aside and follows her lead with empathy.

stem: Professional softball pitcher Rosa Jimenez says, "Once I walk a batter, I always fall apart." Reviewing game charts with her, consultant Will Thornton notices two recent games in which she walked a batter and then retired the side in order. Will uses a solution-focused approach. Which next step is most consistent with that approach?
options: Ask what she did differently in those two games and how she could do more of it
Explore with her when the pattern began and what earlier experiences may be driving it
Work with her to build a new reset routine to replace the habits she uses after walks
Point out that "always" is an overgeneralization and have her dispute the belief
rationales: Solution-focused practice (de Shazer) looks for exceptions, times the problem did not happen, and helps the client identify and repeat what she was already doing that worked.
Tracing the origins of the pattern is problem-focused, insight-oriented work that solution-focused consultants deliberately avoid, however collaboratively it is done.
A new routine may help eventually, but it bypasses solutions she has already shown she can produce; solution-focused work builds on existing strengths first.
Labeling "always" as an overgeneralization and disputing it is cognitive restructuring. It may draw on the same games, but through a cognitive-behavioral rather than solution-focused lens.
takeaway: Solution-focused consultants find exceptions and help clients do more of what already works.

stem: After a disappointing World Cup race, elite cross-country skier Freya Lind dwells only on her errors and has avoided reviewing the race. Her consultant, Carlos Mendes, grounds his work in Orlick's research-based elements of excellence. In their debrief a few days later, which approach best reflects that model?
options: Let her decide when to review the race, and use this debrief to plan her recovery block
Review her split times with her, then pinpoint the errors that cost her the most time
Set process goals with her for the next race so that her attention turns to what's ahead
Guide her to name what went well, what to adjust, and the lessons to take into training
rationales: Respecting her timing is well meant, but she is already avoiding the review. Orlick's model treats constructive evaluation as a core element, so deferring it indefinitely leaves her focus on errors unchallenged.
Split data are useful, but a review aimed only at the costliest errors reinforces the error-focused dwelling she already shows instead of the balanced evaluation the model calls for.
Forward-looking process goals matter, but setting them without first drawing lessons from this race skips the evaluation step that should inform them.

Orlick's elements of excellence include constructive evaluation: after each performance, identify what went well, what needs adjusting, and the lessons to carry forward. This balances her error focus and turns the race into usable learning.
takeaway: Constructive evaluation balances what went well with what to adjust and turns each performance into lessons for training.

stem: Consultant Thandiwe Mokoena is leading a workshop for youth club coaches, several of whom say mental strengths such as confidence, focus, and coping with pressure are "things kids either have or don't." Drawing on research into the psychological characteristics of Olympic champions, which message should she emphasize?
options: These strengths are fairly stable by adolescence, so coaches should prioritize screening for them
These strengths emerge mainly through elite competition, so youth coaches can focus on physical skills
These strengths develop over years with help from coaches and parents, so coaches can foster them
These strengths are best taught by a sport psychology specialist, so coaches should refer athletes
rationales: Treating mental strengths as fixed by adolescence and screening for them reflects a talent-selection view that the research does not support; champions described these strengths as developed over time.
Champions reported that these strengths were shaped well before the elite level, so postponing them until elite competition misses the developmental window the research highlights.

Research on U.S. Olympic champions (Gould and colleagues) found that psychological characteristics such as confidence, focus, and coping with pressure were developed over many years, with coaches, parents, and the wider environment playing key roles. Coaches can intentionally build them.

Specialists can contribute, but the research identified coaches and parents as central influences on how these strengths developed. Handing the job off entirely to a specialist misses the message that coaches themselves can build them.
takeaway: Research on Olympic champions shows mental strengths are developed through supportive people and environments, so coaches can build them.
